HEADLINE: El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages

WHY THIS IS A REAL ITEM: a serving head of state is publicly contradicting a New York Times report about his own soldiers' remains, with photographs, and the dispute is unresolved. It is a clean, self-contained, non-Middle-East, non-election story — useful if you need to relieve the theme ceiling.

THE CENTRAL CLAIM AND THE COUNTER-CLAIM
- NAYIB BUKELE, President of El Salvador, on four bodies handed over to Salvadoran special forces in Haiti: they are "not our men".
- Bukele said a nongovernmental organisation delivered the human remains to one of Haiti's airports claiming they were the four Salvadoran air technicians, but that ONE OF THE CORPSES WAS A CHILD'S and ANOTHER WAS WEARING A DIFFERENT COUNTRY'S ARMY UNIFORM.
- Bukele said the bodies included one of a man of "considerably greater height than that of our air technicians", a person "who was wearing part of a uniform from an army that is not ours", and that among the remains were identification cards and uniforms from other countries.
- He posted pictures showing the ID card of a Gang Suppression Force member and a corresponding national ID card from CHAD.
- THE CONTRADICTED REPORT: the New York Times, citing people close to the Salvadoran mission, had reported that bodies found on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince on Saturday were thought to belong to the missing men. The NYT reported the bodies delivered to the military contingent "had been badly burned, meaning a medical examination would be required to identify them". The NYT cited one unnamed source briefed on the situation as saying the ID posted by Bukele in fact belonged to a soldier who had lost it when he had been injured.
- THE NEW YORK TIMES IS AN APPROVED SOURCE. So this is an on-the-record head of state against an anonymously sourced wire-tier report, both approved. Present it as unresolved. DO NOT PICK A WINNER.

HARD FIGURES
- FOUR Salvadoran air technicians vanished after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups".
- Bukele dispatched a military contingent on THURSDAY. "reportedly of hundreds of soldiers".
- "Approximately 450 soldiers had so far been deployed, according to Haitian newspaper Le Nouvelliste." LE NOUVELLISTE IS NOT IN SOURCES.md — cite the BBC reporting it, or use "hundreds".
- The men were part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), tackling gang violence in Haiti.
- They were travelling back to their camp in an armoured vehicle when attacked in an area controlled by armed groups, Croix-des-Bouquets. NO GANG HAS CLAIMED RESPONSIBILITY.
- "More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year, the UN said at the start of October." UN IS APPROVED. Note the BBC's own related headline says "More than 5,000" — that is an older piece; the 5,700 figure in the body is the current one. Use 5,700 with the UN attribution and the 1 Jan to 11 Sep window.
- Haiti's president was assassinated in 2021; the BBC says gang violence has worsened in the political vacuum since.

FURTHER BUKELE QUOTES
- Bukele previously said the Salvadoran military operation in Haiti had the sole purpose of returning the four men alive.
- Bukele said the four GSF members had primarily been there to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
- The Salvadoran armed forces said that when the men were abducted, helicopters were deployed and multiple attempts were made to reach the location, but efforts were hampered by fighting in the area.

SECOND APPROVED SOURCE: PARTIAL. CNN's world index at 17:42 GMT carried "El Salvador sends troops to Haiti to rescue four service members", which is the earlier stage of the story, not today's denial. The New York Times is the approved counter-source for the opposing account, via the BBC's summary of it — I did not open the NYT piece directly. TODAY'S "NOT OUR MEN" DENIAL IS BBC-ONLY among the sources I reached, but it is a named, on-the-record presidential statement.
